item.title: Your modern motherboard still needs a chip designed for decades-old PC hardware
item.itunes:title: Your modern motherboard still needs a chip designed for decades-old PC hardware
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever your motherboard reads a temperature sensor or reports a fan speed, the underlying computation is happening not on your CPU but on a chip that came about back in the 1980s. The Super I/O chip is a dedicated microchip on your motherboard managing low-bandwidth I/O devices. Back then, this meant serial and parallel ports, PS/2 controllers, and floppy disk controllers.

These legacy ports are gone from modern PCs, but the Super I/O chip still manages key functions, namely system monitoring and power management. Instead of going extinct with legacy hardware, it evolved to take on newer responsibilities.

Your motherboard still can't do one thing a 20-year-old sound card could, and BioShock proves it

And it's all Windows' fault.

23
By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

Super I/O was built for a PC that looked nothing like yours

It brought multiple controllers together

Credit: Unsplash

Before Super I/O chips showed up on computers around four decades ago, expansion cards were used to add basic ports like serial, parallel, and floppy disk controllers via the ISA bus. As manufacturing costs dropped around the late 1980s and early 1990s, vendors started integrating these multi-court circuits into a single Super I/O chip soldered on the motherboard.

Gradually, every single one of these jobs became extinct on newer PCs. Floppy disks became museum pieces, parallel-port printers gave way to USB models, and PS/2 keyboards and mice went away, too. The chip that was purpose-built to consolidate legacy device connections should have disappeared along with them, but it has lived on to this day.

This cheap tool saved me more times than I can count, but motherboards don't support it anymore

Your motherboard probably has a legacy port that was once very useful for troubleshooting, but isn't anymore

1
By  Ty Sherback

It picked up newer jobs along the way

You probably make use of it everyday

Somewhere along the way, the Super I/O chip picked up a second job that eventually became more important than its primary one. Newer Super I/O chips absorbed hardware monitoring duties that they're handling even today. Handling the communication with temperature, fan speed, voltage, and chassis intrusion detection sensors became the job of the Super I/O chip.

Over the years, the communication bus changed from the ISA bus to PCI and then to the LPC (Low Pin Count) bus, a simple and low-cost interface. However, the responsibilities of the chip have remained the same ever since. You can find it on your motherboard typically near the PCIe slots — it's a square or rectangular chip with an ITE or Nuvoton label.

I found four obscure motherboard headers that serve almost no purpose, but manufacturers keep shipping them anyway

Your motherboard has headers you probably have no use for

6
By  Abhinav Raj

Super I/O has evolved physically, but remains functionally the same

It's not always a dedicated microchip

From expansion cards to dedicated microchips on motherboards, the functionality handled by Super I/O chips kept switching form factors. Today, they still exist as discrete microchips, but they can also be found integrated into the primary chipset on some motherboards. On server boards, many management tasks are offloaded to the Baseboard Management Controller (BMC), but a compact Super I/O controller can still be found.

On laptops, Super I/O chips are present in the form of embedded controllers, and perform many of the same functions. Since temperature and fan speed monitoring are basic functions on any modern PC, the Super I/O chip will remain on motherboards in one form or another.

I'd love to see this one laptop feature on all motherboards

Create your own I/O.

4
By  Rich Edmonds

Modern motherboards have more than a few legacy holdovers

The Super I/O chip isn't the only decades-old remnant on modern motherboards. The serial header and PS/2 port can still be found on your PC despite being useless for the average user. That said, they have a reason to exist, whether it's for latency or troubleshooting benefits by enthusiasts and technicians.

item.title: I ditched Chrome's password manager for this open-source app and I'm never going back
item.itunes:title: I ditched Chrome's password manager for this open-source app and I'm never going back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My biggest fear isn’t spiders, heights, cockroaches, or even the faintest sight of blood. It’s needing to log into an account while someone watches me cycle through every password I’ve ever used, hoping one of them magically works.

It’s no fun confidently typing a password, getting told it’s wrong, trying three more variations of it, and eventually surrendering to the Forgot password? button. Despite having the terrible habit of either reusing the same password across multiple accounts or making tiny variations of one I already know, I still somehow manage to forget which version I used where.

It’s a habit I’m actively trying to unlearn, but with or without it, a password manager is one utility I can’t imagine surviving without. While I’ve relied on Chrome’s password manager (and Apple's Passwords app on my iPhone) for far too long, I recently started wondering whether convenience was the only reason I was still using them. So, I finally went looking for something better, and ended up switching to Proton Pass.

I can finally use the same password manager everywhere

Proton Pass works wherever I do

If you go through my XDA author page, you’ll notice that I am always switching between browsers. Though a lot of the browsers I’ve tested before are Chromium-based, I’ve also spent plenty of time with Firefox-based alternatives, including Zen Browser, which is currently my daily driver.

I also currently use an iPhone, and that means my passwords have historically been split across ecosystems. Some end up saved to my Google account, while most make their way into Apple’s Passwords app. It works, but it also means I have to remember where I saved a login before I can even worry about remembering the login itself!

Proton Pass gets rid of that problem. Instead of choosing a password manager based on whichever browser or device I happen to be using, I can use the same vault everywhere. There’s an extension for Firefox and Chromium-based browsers, a Safari extension, and dedicated apps for iOS, macOS, Windows, Android, and Linux. On my iPhone, I can also set Proton Pass as an AutoFill provider, so my saved logins show up in apps and websites just like they would with Apple’s built-in solution.

Proton Pass actually lets me manage my passwords

This is what a real password manager feels like

When I hear the word “password manager,” I’d expect to be able to do a little more than just save passwords and scroll through one massive list of them. If you’ve used Chrome’s password manager, that’s all it really lets you do. When you’re signing into an app or website, it asks if you’d like to save the password, and from there, that login simply joins everything else you’ve saved over the years.

You can search through those passwords when you need one, but there’s no real way to organize them into folders or separate vaults. Whether it’s my real or digital life, I have a terrible hoarding habit. I’ve never thrown away a flower I’ve gotten from someone, and the same largely applies to my online accounts. If I signed up for some random website seven years ago and haven’t touched it since, there’s a very good chance its login is still sitting somewhere in my password manager.

Once you've accumulated hundreds of logins like that, one giant list gets messy extremely quickly. My life is currently spread across work, college, and personal stuff, and I use completely different tools for each. My work accounts have nothing to do with my university portals, and neither really belongs mixed in with streaming services, shopping accounts, social media, and everything else I’ve signed up for over the years.

Proton Pass handles this much better by letting me split everything into separate vaults. I can keep work, college, and personal logins apart instead of treating every password I own as part of one giant pile.

Proton Pass’s aliases feature is a lifesaver

Every random website gets a fake email now

My work involves a lot of testing random apps, and of course, there are very few apps that let you get far without creating an account first. This means I'm constantly handing my email address over to services I might use once for some testing and never open again.

Now, a lot of the apps I try are fairly niche, and I don’t necessarily know much about the company behind them before signing up. Giving every single one my actual email address has never sat particularly well with me, especially when there’s a good chance I’ll delete the app 20 minutes later.

Proton Pass’s aliases give me a much better option. Whenever I’m signing up for something new, I can generate a unique email address instead of handing over my real one. These aliases are essentially forwarding addresses. Anything sent to them still lands in my regular inbox, but the service I signed up for never sees the actual email address behind them.

I replaced all my productivity apps with Proton for a month and here’s how it went

The pros and cons of relying solely on Proton apps

9
By  Parth Shah

That means I still get confirmation emails, password resets, and anything else I need without maintaining a completely separate inbox. If an app starts spamming me, or I simply stop using it, I can disable that specific alias without affecting my real email address or any of my other accounts. On Proton's free tier, you get up to ten aliases pointing to a single email address. If you upgrade to the paid account, you get an unlimited number of aliases and custom domains as well.

Proton Pass has an incredibly capable free tier

I don’t particularly like the idea of needing to pay to store my passwords safely, and the good thing about Proton Pass is that I don’t have to. Its free plan lets me store unlimited logins and notes, sync them across unlimited devices, use passkeys, generate passwords, and access Proton Pass through its browser, desktop, and mobile apps.

There are still reasons to pay. Proton reserves features like unlimited aliases, additional vaults, its built-in 2FA authenticator, file attachments, and more advanced security features for its paid plans. But none of those restrictions stop the free version from doing the most important job of a password manager!

item.title: Opera's new automatic VPN toggle makes keeping your data safe a lot easier
item.itunes:title: Opera's new automatic VPN toggle makes keeping your data safe a lot easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Opera's built-in VPN auto-activates on insecure/public Wi-Fi to encrypt your traffic.
  • Rolling out now in the US and France; you can disable it if you prefer manual VPN control.
  • Opera's VPN keeps zero logs and runs automatically to make online privacy effortless on the go.

VPNs are a lot more useful than skirting around pesky geoblocking checks on websites. In fact, if you're only using it to watch TV shows and movies in another country, you're actually sitting on a valuable privacy tool without realising it. Fortunately, Opera's new feature is here to help people stay safe without having to lift a finger.

Opera's built-in VPN can now automatically turn on when connecting to insecure networks

It's only available in the US and France right now

Credit: Opera

In an emailed press release, Opera gave us a sneak peek into its brand new feature releasing today. It capitalizes on Opera's built-in VPN (which Opera points out is a feature some big browsers still don't have by default) to keep you safe when you connect to a potentially dangerous network.

It's very easy to use; in fact, if it works as advertised, you shouldn't have to do any work whatsoever. When Opera detects that you've connected to a public Wi-Fi hotspot or an insecure router, it will immediately flip the switch to turn on the VPN. This ensures all the data going to and from your laptop is properly encrypted and sent through a tunnel, preventing people or software from spying on what you're doing. And given how Opera claims its VPN saves zero logs, you won't need to worry about it spying on you, either.

Arjan van Leeuwen, Head of Opera One Engineering at Opera, had the following to say:

“From the very start, all the way back in 2016, we believed that online privacy should be effortless and straightforward - especially when connecting to public networks while out and about. Ten years later, our thesis still holds: VPNs are a vital part of users’ digital hygiene. That’s why we continue supporting and improving our free browser VPN, making sure that Opera users always have the tools they need, when they need them.”

The feature is rolling out right now to users in the US and France, and if you're not a fan of it, you can always disable it and handle the VPN changes yourself.

item.title: Canonical is speeding up Ubuntu's kernel updates because it's drowning in AI-discovered bugs
item.itunes:title: Canonical is speeding up Ubuntu's kernel updates because it's drowning in AI-discovered bugs
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • LLMs have massively increased CVE reports, overwhelming maintainers.
  • Canonical now bundles updates into a unified two-week cycle to handle the flood.
  • It mirrors the Linux kernel's recent discovery of a "new normal" for AI-generated bug reports.

Whether or not LLMs belong in an open-source project, whether they're used for content generation or for finding bugs, is an ongoing debate within the FOSS scene right now. Some communities have banned it, while others have adopted the new tech, although they've had to adapt to a new way of doing things. Such is the case with Canonical, which has announced a new two-week unified patch cycle for Ubuntu because LLMs can't stop finding bugs in the kernel.

Canonical squashes its Ubuntu update cycle into a two-week cycle

There are just too many reports coming in

Credit: Canonical

As spotted by OMG Ubuntu, Canonical has announced its new update cycle. It reveals that maintainers have recently been swamped with more Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures reports (CVEs) than ever before, and there's no prize for guessing why:

The recent explosion in the volume of CVEs is fueled by artificial intelligence: large language models (LLMs) and specialized AI agents have transformed bug discovery from a manual, time-intensive process into a highly automated engine. Additionally, the upstream kernel community became its own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) and assigned CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifiers to thousands of bugs, arguing that at the kernel level, almost any type of bug that can affect a running system, could potentially be classified as a vulnerability.

This, in turn, has prompted developers to speed up the process of getting patches out the door. Right now, they're swamped with CVEs, so they're moving away from a regular update every four weeks and a security patch every two weeks. Now, everything's getting bundled into one big two-week update cycle, and you can see its timeline in the chart above.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

27
By  Simon Batt

Maintainers drowning in LLM-discovered issues is by no means new

It has been a constant presence for the Linux kernel recently

The thing is, Ubuntu is by no means an outlier here. The Linux kernel itself has been wading through a sea of bug reports recently, and it doesn't seem like it'll die down any time soon.

We first saw signs that something was amiss back during the Linux 7.0 release candidates. Linus Torvalds noticed a spike in the number of bug reports, which made each release candidate larger than they usually are; however, the bugs being found weren't serious ones, which didn't justify delaying 7.0's release. Torvalds would go on to release 7.0 on time.

Things came to a head in the Linux 7.1 release, when Torvalds realized 7.0 was not a fluke, and the release candidates were still really big. Even worse, bug reports were coming in that either used secure channels for menial changes or duplicated other bug reports, making it "almost entirely unmanageable."

Torvalds chalked this trend up to AI assistants automatically spotting, reporting, and fixing bugs, which ended up in larger changelists than before. Torvalds would crown this "the new normal," and has since adapted to handle the influx, much like how Canonical is feeling out its own "new normal" right now.

Linus Torvalds is right about AI coding, and the backlash misses the point

AI code should be allowed, and you should be held responsible for it.

item.title: I switched Ubuntu's desktop to Cinnamon for speed, but the real upgrade was how I work
item.itunes:title: I switched Ubuntu's desktop to Cinnamon for speed, but the real upgrade was how I work
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 is not the most friendly option for an old PC these days, and many (myself included) will recommend switching to Linux to extend the life of a laptop. But Linux distros aren't all the same, and while Ubuntu is a popular pick, it's not without its downsides.

System requirements for Ubuntu have risen a lot over the years, and that's in big part thanks to the GNOME desktop environment it ships with. That, paired with some of the other problems I have with GNOME, pushed me to switch to another desktop to make things feel faster. But it wasn't quite the upgrade I was expecting.

Ubuntu has become bloated

GNOME is not exactly lightweight

Ubuntu's GNOME desktop is known primarily for its ease of use, and the fact that it makes it easier for a newcomer to get used to Linux. It has other benefits, of course, with extensive customization options enabled by GNOME extensions, and a generally robust set of software tools bundled in.

However, all of that has come at the cost of performance. Ubuntu now requires at least 6GB of RAM, and on my 8-year-old laptop, things do feel like they could be smoother. This is still a capable laptop with 16GB of RAM, and I'm not saying GNOME is unusable by any means, but it could use a slight performance bump.

Plus, there are other aspects I don't love about GNOME that make things feel slower by nature of being more cumbersome. I don't really like the full-screen app launcher and search UI, the unified system menu makes it feel like it takes longer to change certain settings, and so on. Plus, the lack of customization options with GNOME extensions is a problem as those extensions can cause stability issues when GNOME gets updated.

Ubuntu is the reason Windows users don't want to switch to Linux

First impressions matter

311
By  João Carrasqueira

Thankfully, unlike Windows, Ubuntu lets me change my desktop entirely, and on this hardware, I had a few options. I'm sure I could still run a more modern desktop like KDE Plasma or COSMIC here, but for the sake of improving performance, a lighter option such as Cinnamon seemed like the best route to take.

Cinnamon immediately feels better

But speed is only a small part of it

Booting into Cinnamon, things felt different, but not quite how I expected. While Cinnamon is still only offering experimental support for the Wayland compositor, things feel just a little bit snappier. Cinnamon's apps may launch and feel a little bit faster, but the biggest difference in perceived speed comes from how much easier to do just about anything (at least on this hardware).

The desktop paradigm in Cinnamon just feels more natural, and things feel more accessible overall. The app launcher acts just like the Start menu on Windows (especially before Windows 11), and I can search for apps without having to take over the entire screen. The power options have their own dedicated menu that feels much faster to use than GNOME's UI, and you can say a lot of the same thing about all of the quick settings available in GNOME's unified flyout.

I tried out these 5 Linux desktop environments that aren't GNOME or KDE, and they're surprisingly decent

But KDE Plasma is still the king of desktop environments

10
By  Ayush Pande

Maybe it's the familiarity, as a former Windows user, but things just feel far more natural here, and I can get things done more quickly. It's not necessarily improving my PC's performance, but it does improve mine.

I also like how many more customization options Linux Mint offers out of the box. I can download and install themes, add panels to each edge of the screen with their own dedicated widgets, or add "desklets" directly to the desktop. It's a very customizable platform that doesn't require me to jump through as many hoops.

There are other options

Though they have other downsides

If you really want performance gains on Ubuntu because you're hardware-constrained, Cinnamon may not be the best option for you. It is lighter than GNOME, but not as much as you might think. You can try even lighter alternatives like Xfce or LXQT if you really want to see resource usage go down and a smoother experience.

However, that comes at the cost of a UI that tends to feel ancient and lacks some of the modern conveniences that, personally, I'm not willing to give up. Xfce just isn't visually appealing, and unlike nearly every other desktop, the Meta key doesn't even open the app launcher or a search bar, so things feel a little more cumbersome.

I gave my old Chromebook new life by making it look like Windows 95 using the XFCE desktop environment

A blast from the past using Linux.

4
By  Ethan Meyerowitz

Of course, these are desktops you can learn, and if you're really starved for smoother performance, these are probably the best option that don't require you to reinstall your operating system altogether.

You may want an entirely different distro

That's where real performance gains lie

Ultimately, however, if you really want the best performance possible from your hardware, it may be best to ditch Ubuntu completely and just use a lighter distro from the start. If you want to use Cinnamon with an overall lighter platform, you can install Linux Mint; it's the operating system Cinnamon is designed for in the first place, and while it's still loosely based on Ubuntu, it's just a far lighter platform overall.

The thing about installing a different desktop is that you may still have leftover services and apps from the original desktop, but a full distro like Mint can ship Cinnamon with all the appropriate apps and services that match it better and offer better performance in the end. You can try deleting the original desktop on Ubuntu after installing a new one, but that can be a pretty tedious task in itself.

Linux Mint's new kernel cleanup feature makes it even more appealing for people escaping Windows

When learning how to use Linux, less is sometimes more.

6
By  Simon Batt

It's all about how much time you have. If you can take the time to back up your files and start over with a new distro, or you can split the partition and move your files over, I recommend a whole new distro. But if not, just switching desktops can still make a difference.

Replacing GNOME is always a good idea

Even if it isn't for the performance gains, replacing Ubuntu's GNOME desktop is always a valid strategy in my book. GNOME is simply too clunky and rigid for my liking, and you can get a better experience with almost any of the alternatives on the market. While an entirely different distro is even better, it just depends on how comfortable you are with that kind of transition.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]

I usually bounce between LM Studio for casual chat, AnythingLLM for RAG workflows, llama.cpp for cutting-edge features, and a couple more. So you end up with a bunch of different tools for different jobs.

Unsloth is only a name I've been recognizing through their quants. The UD-tagged GGUFs on Hugging Face have been feeding my LM Studio setup for as long as I've had it, and I'd generally trust one of their dynamic quants over pretty much any equivalent. When they launched their own desktop app in August, I figured if anyone was going to build a good local AI app, it would be the team already making the models I run.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

If you've ever downloaded a GUFF with "UD" in the name, you've already used Unsloth

The company behind the quants now has its own app

Unsloth as a name might already ring a bell even if you've never installed anything from them. It started as an open-source Python library from two brothers, Daniel and Michael Han, that made fine-tuning LLMs roughly two times faster with about 70% less VRAM and no accuracy loss. That reputation is why anyone doing fine-tuning without cloud budgets usually end up on it, or if you simply have more limited hardware.

Along the way they also became one of the biggest publishers of GGUF quants on Hugging Face. Those "Unsloth Dynamic" files (the ones with UD-Q4_K_XL or UD-IQ1_S in the filename) are theirs, and most of us have probably been running them for a minute now without really thinking about where they come from.

Unsloth Desktop launched in beta on 10 August 2026 for Mac, Windows, and Linux, and it's free and open-source. It's the first time the team has shipped a native app for running and training models locally, but the underlying tech is the same tech they've been building for years. So going by their track record, I had a good feeling about this one before even installing it.

The philosophy is pretty clearly that it's meant to be one workspace for the whole local AI stack. So you've got your chat and model management, plus fine-tuning, plus generation, plus agent connections and remote access, all in the same place now.

I tested every tiny local LLM worth running, and only three survived the cut

Small models are doing more than they should

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Downloading Unsloth Quants from inside the Unsloth app

Cutting out the middle step

The model hub is Unsloth's own catalog, curated by them, filterable by what actually fits my hardware. It also picked up every model I already had sitting on disk from my other runners, so there was no reimporting or folder hunting required. This seems like a small thing but it means switching over to Unsloth is quick and easy.

Unsloth uses a technique called Dynamic quantization that selectively quantizes different layers at different bit levels instead of squashing everything down uniformly. That's why a UD-Q4_K_XL will often outperform a standard Q4 while being roughly the same size or a bit smaller. Their newer Dynamic v3.0 quants (which the Model Hub surfaces first) claim over 10% higher accuracy than other quants of the same size, and Unsloth is one of very few sources I'd actually trust for sub-4-bit quants of huge MoE models like DeepSeek or Kimi.

Because this is Unsloth's own app, you also get Day Zero support for new releases. If a big model drops it's usually running here before LM Studio's catalog has indexed it. LM Studio's hub is a Hugging Face pass-through so the good dynamic quants are there but you have to hunt for them. Ollama's registry lags behind and doesn't reliably carry them. And AnythingLLM doesn't touch model management at all.

Gemma 4 is lightweight, runs on my 16GB laptop, and costs $0 to keep me productive offline

There's no laptop I own that doesn't have it

9
By  Abhinav Raj

The amount of control you get is wild

Whatever you want to tweak, there's probably a toggle for it

Model params are where LM Studio has historically been the strong one, and Unsloth's per-model configuration panel is at least as deep. It has KV cache dtype, speculative decoding, tensor parallelism, batch and micro-batch size, GPU memory allocation and a VRAM budget slider, a chat template editor, and extra CLI arguments passed through to llama-server.

Then there's the chat behavior settings, which is a category LM Studio and Ollama barely touch. Queue vs steer follow-up behavior when you send during a response, plain text vs formatted composer, auto-compact for long chats that hit the context limit, condensing long pastes into .txt attachments automatically, and remembering settings per model. These are small ergonomic things you probably wouldn't really notice until you've been using it for a couple of days.

The UI itself is also super customizable, with adjustable chat width, desktop scaling, a compact composer mode, and a floating system monitor showing CPU / RAM / VRAM / disk usage live. And then there are the permission controls. Every tool call, whether that's web search, code execution, file access, or an MCP action, has a permissions layer with Approve, Always Approve, or Deny. This is the same as in Claude Code or Codex, and not something LM Studio or Ollama offer, and AnythingLLM only sort of implements.

Lastly, there's parallel chatting. A new chat can start while the previous one is still generating, each conversation gets its own progress indicator and stop button, so I don't have to sit here and wait on slow responses before moving onto the next session.

I ran Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.5 for the same local tasks, and one pulled miles ahead

Pitting them against each other to find the best one for my workflow

12
By  Nolen Jonker

Fine-tuning and dataset building

The full local AI loop

This is where the comparison to LM Studio, Ollama, and AnythingLLM stops making sense because none of them do training at all. Unsloth Desktop ships with a full no-code training pipeline - training here means fine-tuning, which is where you take an existing open-source model and teach it on your own data so it starts responding how you need it to for your specific use case, whether it's your domain, brand voice, or whatever task you need it for.

Fine-tuning isn't something I do or need every day, but this is definitely one of those nice-to-haves. The Train tab handles QLoRA (4-bit adapters, low VRAM), LoRA (16-bit, better quality), full fine-tuning, and continued pretraining, all using the Unsloth kernels that make training two times faster with 70% less VRAM in the library. So you pick your base model, drop in your dataset (CSV, JSONL, PDF, DOCX, TXT, MD), and pick a method.

Then there's Data Recipes, which pairs nicely with training and I just think it's a pretty cool feature. It's a visual node-based workflow builder for turning raw documents into training-ready datasets, powered by NVIDIA's NeMo Data Designer. For my design projects, this means I can basically point it at my past briefs and references and let it structure a dataset for me based on that. Unfortunately, training locally still needs the hardware to back it up. My RTX 3070 with 8GB of VRAM handles QLoRA on smaller models, but I'm obviously not fine-tuning a 27B in here.

I ran the same local LLM on an RTX 5070 laptop and one with an iGPU, and the difference was smaller than I expected

You don't need an expensive GPU to start running local AI.

10
By  Yash Patel

Sloth just did what the others never got around to

There will still be workflows I reach LM Studio, Ollama, and AnythingLLM for, but most of those tasks can now happen in one window with Unsloth. The one thing I'd add is that this app being in beta means updates are landing at a pretty rapid pace, so whatever it's missing today probably has a good chance of appearing in a release note the next time.

Unsloth

item.title: I spent $20 on an old Blu-ray player and rediscovered the joy of physical media
item.itunes:title: I spent $20 on an old Blu-ray player and rediscovered the joy of physical media
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently bought an older Blu-ray player for my spare guest room for around $20, and I realized how much fun physical media can be. I started remembering the days when streaming media was a thing and all we had was physical media, including carefully wiping smudges off dirty discs with a microfiber cloth and waiting in anticipation for the menu to appear so I could watch a movie or show.

I also remember roommates who, like with CDs, put the wrong disc in the wrong case, and getting irked when someone scratched up a favorite title. I liked checking out the cool artwork, and I built my library on a series of case holders and bookshelves instead of a server.

More Special Features

Additional special features digital streaming versions don't have

When I started collecting Blu-rays back in the day, I always looked forward to the extra special features. Interviews with the actors, scenes that didn't make the cut or alternate endings, how special effects were done, and more. Those were all reasons to buy Blu-ray over DVD — not just the picture quality, but the extra features you could get.

Since Blu-ray holds more data, you could access more features. Even today, some old-school 1080p Blu-rays include special features that digital purchases don't. Plus, with streaming and digital media, the extra features vary by the store you buy the digital version from. I have a digital copy of a movie I bought from Apple, which has exciting extras other versions don't.

I compared the same movie on Blu-ray and streaming, and I wasn’t prepared for the difference

The difference was like 1080p Blu-ray and UHD 4K Blu-ray.

22
By  Brian Burgess

I own the media

A virtual locker could vanish

I've always been happy to know I can turn to my physical Blu-ray when a movie vanishes from streaming. The same goes for buying digital copies of movies, organizing them in your digital locker, and then having them suddenly disappear. I do find it convenient that when I buy a Blu-ray, I get a code for the digital version via Movies Anywhere. But what if it were the other way around?

Instead of getting something tangible I can hold in my hands when I buy a digital movie, I'm essentially renting the right to view it. I like having media I can hold in my hands and know that I truly own. I can back them up to a NAS or server and stream them under my control. I don't have to worry about some company's servers or connections going down. I have to worry about my own server, but even if my drives fail, I still own the original Blu-ray of my movies or shows.

I thought all Blu-ray drives were the same until I found the perfect one for ripping physical media to Plex

All Blu-ray drives aren't created equal when you're backing up 4K movies for self-hosted media servers.

By  Brian Burgess

Picture quality wins

Even on 1080p Blu-ray discs

My old Blu-ray player doesn't have the laser or hardware to play UHD 4K discs, but that's fine because it can upscale to 4K. I still notice a difference between the 1080p resolution coming from the old player and a 1080p compressed stream. Like UHD 4K discs, a 1080p Blu-ray disc has more bandwidth for video (up to 40Mbps). A 1080p stream is typically compressed to around 10Mbps.

Also, a player with 4K upscaling means that while it doesn't add 4K detail, the player takes the 1920x1080 disc image and scales it to 3840x2160, which is great if you are like me and connect it to an older 4K display TV. More data per pixel preserves scene textures, shadows, motion, and bright colors better on the screen. Also, the player is backward compatible, so I can watch my old movies and shows from my old DVD collection.

An ad-free player

Streaming is great once you get past the ads to watch something

One of the cool things about streaming services is I can always find something to watch — once I get past the rows of ads. With my Blu-ray player, I still have plenty to watch and don't have to sift through endless ad banners and animated ads on typical streaming sticks. I pop the disc in and go straight to the menu screen, except for a select few rental copies that wandered into my collection and have trailers for upcoming Blu-ray releases.

My Blu-ray collection isn't as expansive as a streaming library, but it's what I like and want to watch. Opening the shiny black box to reveal the disc tray feels nostalgic and gives a stay-home, watch-a-movie feel, rather than sitting at home and binging Netflix. I haven't timed it, but I would guess the time it takes to insert a disc and watch a movie is similar to searching for something to watch on a clunky streaming service.

4K Blu-ray already has a successor, and it isn't what I expected

A 200TB experimental optical disc could dwarf 4K Blu-ray, but data centers and archival storage will likely benefit first.

25
By  Jeff Butts

A $20 Blu-ray player rekindles fondness for physical discs

I've gotten a lot from my $20 investment, and rediscovered my love of owning physical copies of my favorite movies and shows. I found my $20 player at a pawn shop and talked it down from $50. It also has YouTube and Netflix apps built in, which can turn a dumb TV into a smart TV.

But you can find them at garage sales (where I bought a cheap AV receiver to replace a soundbar), thrift stores, library sales, or online markets like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist. If you're lucky, you'll find a UHD 4K player for somewhere near $20.

A virtual locker could vanish

Also, a player with 4K upscaling means that while it doesn't add 4K detail, the player takes the 1920x1080 disc image and scales it to 3840x2160, which is great if you are like me and connect it to an older 4K display TV. 4K Blu-ray already has a successor, and it isn't what I expected

But you can find them at garage sales (where I bought a cheap AV receiver to replace a soundbar), thrift stores, library sales, or online markets like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist. If you're lucky, you'll find a UHD 4K player for somewhere near $20.

item.title: This free open-source tool beats Windows Task Manager at its own game
item.itunes:title: This free open-source tool beats Windows Task Manager at its own game
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Task Manager is one of those things I open on Windows without even thinking twice whenever an app or game stops responding, or my PC suddenly feels sluggish for no reason. It's reassuring to know that I can press Ctrl + Shift + Esc at any point and hit End Task on an app that just won't close normally, or see what's hogging my CPU or RAM. And if that's all you do in Task Manager, you probably don't have anything to complain about.

But if you're anything like me and like digging a little deeper, Task Manager doesn't show nearly as much information as you'd like. That's exactly what convinced me to try System Informer when a gaming friend recommended it recently. It's a completely free and open-source tool that looks like Task Manager on steroids. I've only been using it for a week, but it's already convinced me to set up a keyboard shortcut so I can bring it up as quickly as Task Manager.

I launch all my apps with a keyboard shortcut — here's how you can too

It's easier than you'd think

2
By  Anurag Singh

System Informer tells me much more about every process

Task Manager barely scratches the surface

The first thing you see when you open System Informer is a long list of all the processes running on your PC, similar to what you see in Task Manager, except it's much more detailed and overwhelming at first. System Informer organizes processes into a proper parent-child tree with highlighting that makes different types of processes easier to distinguish. You can also add a ridiculous number of columns if you want to by right-clicking any column header and clicking Choose Columns. You can add details for disk writes, I/O history, GPU dedicated bytes, and more. I haven't added anything myself yet, but I like having the option to track down something specific if needed.

Double-clicking a process is where Task Manager gets left behind because it does nothing. System Informer, on the other hand, gives you dedicated views for individual threads, GPU, memory, handles, and other detailed information. The Modules tab, for instance, lets me see every DLL a process has loaded. I'm sure most of you don't need this level of detail every time you open Task Manager, but when you're actively trying to troubleshoot something, having all this information in one place can save you a lot of digging around.

It doesn't just replace Task Manager

It's like having several Windows utilities in one app

System Informer also saves you from opening separate utilities whenever the problem isn't obvious from CPU or memory usage. For instance, I can click Find handles or DLLs and search for a specific file to see exactly which process has it open. This is useful when Windows refuses to delete or rename a file because it's being used by another program, but doesn't make it obvious which one. Windows lets you search through associated handles in Resource Monitor, but I like having this functionality built in.

Then, there's the Services tab, similar to the one in Task Manager, but System Informer gives you more information and control without making you open Services.msc separately. I can double-click a service to check its dependencies or change its start type. I also like how its Network view shows me the actual connections each process has open. Even the Disk view is useful, since I can see which processes are actively reading from or writing to specific files without opening Resource Monitor.

Task Manager is still more than enough for most people

But even for the basics, System Informer gives you more options

As much as I've enjoyed using this tool, I don't think everybody needs to replace Task Manager right away. I'm sure most of you just bring it up to end an app that has stopped responding or quickly check what's hogging your CPU or RAM, and Task Manager is perfectly fine for that. As I said earlier, System Informer can feel pretty overwhelming at first and somewhat unnecessary if you don't care about all the extra information it gives you.

However, System Informer still gives you more options for some of those basic tasks. For example, instead of simply terminating a process, you can use Terminate Tree to kill it and all its child processes, which is handy when an app runs several processesin the background. You can also suspend a process without killing it completely and resume it later whenever you want. In the last week that I've used it, I've only used these options twice, but I'd still rather have that extra control whenever I need it.

The keyboard shortcut makes it just as easy to access

Honestly, I would've just gone back to Task Manager if opening System Informer every time felt like an extra step. But I've set up a keyboard shortcut by right-clicking System Informer's shortcut and opening Properties. Now, all I need to do is press Ctrl + Shift + I to bring it up, which is close enough to Ctrl + Shift + Esc that I've been used to since forever. Considering I've only been using it for a week, I'm sure I'll still open Task Manager out of habit every now and then, but I can already see System Informer becoming my default. At the end of the day, it's everything I want from Task Manager, but better in almost every way.

System Informer

item.title: This Anthropic course's prompt formula fixed the one mistake I was making with every AI tool
item.itunes:title: This Anthropic course's prompt formula fixed the one mistake I was making with every AI tool
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using AI tools for some time, switching between services like Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and NotebookLM. But rather than just using the tools, I wanted to understand them on a deeper level.

That's why I took courses from Anthropic and Google to understand how these tools work and how to get the most out of them. During a lesson on how to get helpful responses from Claude, I realized I had been making a crucial mistake: sending generic prompts that produced generic responses.

I replaced my entire AI prompt library with Fabric, and now I can't imagine going back

I wish I found it a year ago

12
By  Anurag Singh

Vague prompts create generic responses

The AI can't just infer what you want

I know to include important context in my prompts for certain tasks, but I also ask AI to do things without enough detail. And I didn't realize just how much this affects the quality of the responses.

During my time using Claude Projects, I saw how powerful context can be when included in project instructions. But I didn't always carry over this knowledge to my general prompts for other tasks. I'm especially guilty of this when using Gemini.
